Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Time: 16:10 PT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Alex (AE, Redwood), Sam (SE, Redwood), Jordan (CTO, Nova Health), Priya (ML Eng), Marcus (Security), Lena (PM)
Links shared: deck: redwood-structured-output.pdf, example repo: github.com/redwood/structured-examples, security pack: redwood-soc2.pdf

Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
Alex: quick run through of JSON mode, how schemas can be enforced, failure modes, and function calling to hit internal services; Sam demoed live pipeline where model returns validated JSON and triggers a tool call to internal triage service.

Action items (captured above) reiterated at end.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcript imperfect in spots):
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna walk through Redwood's structured output + tool calling, especially how you can return strict JSON payloads and then call your services, um, as part of the pipeline.
[00:12] Jordan: Sounds good. We're especially keen on determinism - our downstream sys can't handle missing fields; so schema enforcement is big for us.
[00:20] Sam: Totally. We'll show JSON mode with schema validation and then a guarded function call. Note, the demo uses a small sample dataset, not production traffic.
[00:30] Priya: Quick question - is the schema enforced at the runtime layer or is it post-processed by client side? I think earlier you mentioned server-side validation?
[00:40] Alex: Good Q. We have both. You can enforce server-side schema validation in Redwood Console or API - the runtime will either reject or autocorrect based on settings. There's also a 'soft-validate' mode where you get warnings.
[00:55] Marcus: From security perspective: where do the logs live? audit logs, is that in your system or can we push them to our SIEM?
[01:05] Sam: We stream audit logs to customer endpoints - support for customer-managed S3 or syslog, and we tie into your KMS for encrypting secrets. We'll share integration docs.
[01:17] Jordan: And residency - we need EU only for some datasets. Can you pin region?
[01:24] Alex: Yes, you can pin to regions or use Private deployment (VPC/on-prem). For hosted it can be region-restricted.
[01:30] Lena: Ok let's see the demo.
[01:35] Sam: Alright I'm going to switch to the Console. First slide is the schema definition: simple JSON Schema we attach to a route, you can mark fields required and types. Example: {"patient_id": "string", "triage_level": "integer"} - note the console shows a preview of expected output.
[02:05] Priya: Do you support enums and nested objects?
[02:10] Sam: Yup, enums, nested arrays, patterns, max length, all supported. We also support custom validators - you can plug in a lambda to run extra checks.
[02:20] Alex: One point: when you enforce strict mode, the runtime will return a 422-like error with details; in autocorrect mode it may attempt to coerce types but always include a validation trace.
[02:35] Jordan: That trace - is it stored? we need it for audits.
[02:40] Sam: Yes audit trail w/ validation traces is retained according to retention settings; can be exported.
[02:48] [02:50] Sam: Now switching to function-calling demo. I'll show a sample where model returns JSON matching the schema and we then call an internal triage tool.
[03:02] Alex: Quick note: function calls can be configured to run only after schema validation succeeds, or you can have a fallback.
[03:12] Sam: Ok hitting the endpoint. (typing) ... you may hear some keyboard clatter.
[03:20] [03:25] Sam: Model output arrives, we validate, it's fine, and now Redwood triggers the tool call to our 'triage-service' - you can see the payload in the request inspector.
[03:35] Priya: The payload looked slightly different than the schema - I think the model returned "triage": "high" when we expected a numeric level 3. Is that the autocorrect in action?
[03:45] Sam: Good catch - yes in autocorrect we cast enums/strings to numeric if possible; we log the change. If you want strictness, enable strict mode and it would error instead.
[03:55] Jordan: In our pipeline we need determinism. We can't have silent coercions. So I'd expect strict mode for pilot.
[04:05] Alex: Understood, pilot in strict mode is normal for customers who are piping outputs to clinical workflows.
[04:12] Marcus: How do we handle secrets for function calls - credentials to triage-service?
[04:18] Sam: Redwood can store encrypted secrets in customer KMS or integrate with your HSM. During function call, we inject a short-lived token; the runtime never persists raw creds.
[04:28] Marcus: We need to review the KMS key policy - can you share sample config?
[04:33] Alex: We'll send the KMS integration guide.
[04:36] [04:40] Sam: Now I'm toggling guardrails - we have a 'schema-first' mode, plus prompt-level safety filters. If output violates allowed values or patterns, you can auto-block, redact, or route to human review.
[04:52] Priya: Human review lane - is that a manual UI or can it call our ticketing system?
[04:58] Sam: Both. We have a built-in queue in Console, or the tool call can create a ticket via your API (we demoed Jira integration earlier).
[05:08] Jordan: About latency - does schema validation add significant overhead? our SLAs need sub-300ms median for simple requests.
[05:15] Sam: There's a small overhead ~20-40ms for typical JSON schemas; heavy custom validators or external lambdas will add more. For high throughput you can precompile validators and we cache compiled validators per route.
[05:30] Alex: Also batching affects latency; for single request low-latency paths we favor small batch sizes with priority routing.
[05:38] [05:42] Priya: Can we run a demo on our dataset?
[05:45] Alex: Yes that's part of the pilot. Sam will scope the ingest and success criteria.
[05:50] Sam: I'll need a sample of requests and what you consider a valid output plus edge-case examples.
[05:58] Priya: We'll send that.
[06:02] [06:05] Jordan: Back to reliability - what's the fallback if the primary model is down?
[06:10] Sam: Redwood has smart routing: fallback to a compatible variant or to a cached response for known prefixes. For structured outputs we can also run a lightweight deterministic parser fallback that returns a safe error object so your downstream can handle it gracefully.
[06:25] Jordan: Good, that helps.
[06:28] Lena: A quick nit - can the Console show diff between raw model output and validated JSON?
[06:34] Sam: Yes, the inspector shows raw vs validated, and the validation trace explains each transformation.
[06:40] Marcus: Anything about compliance - do you keep PII? data retention?
[06:45] Alex: Retention is configurable; we offer short retention, longer for audit with encryption. PII handling: you can enable automatic redaction and tokenization for specific fields.
[06:55] Marcus: Do you support SAML SSO + SCIM for provisioning?
[06:59] Alex: Yes.
[07:02] [07:05] Sam: Switching now to an example of function/tool calling with guarded params: we define which keys are allowed to be passed to the tool; anything else gets stripped. For example, the triage call only gets patient_id and triage_level, not raw_notes.
[07:18] Priya: That's important - we don't want PHI leakage to 3rd party tools.
[07:22] Sam: Exactly. We'll show a policy rule in Console: allow-list of keys, plus regex filters.
[07:30] [07:35] Jordan: On the API side: is this available in REST and SDKs?
[07:40] Alex: Yes, SDKs for Python/JS, and REST endpoints. We'll share code snippets after call.
[07:46] [07:50] Sam: (loads a sample Python snippet) here you define schema in YAML, attach to route, example: route.post('/triage', schema=...) then client.call(..., mode='json', strict=true)
[08:02] Priya: Can we version schema? We will need versioned changes.
[08:06] Sam: Yup schema versions and rollout policies -you can do canary for schema changes. We also support compatibility checks.
[08:14] Jordan: Pricing quick Q - does function calling add cost?
[08:18] Alex: Function calls are a small marginal cost - we bill compute + small per-call integration fee; we'll include specifics in pricing deck.
[08:26] Marcus: Any notes on multi-tenancy for Dedicated vs Private deployments?
[08:32] Alex: Dedicated gives you reserved GPUs and isolation; Private gives a customer-managed control plane (VPC or on-prem). Both support the same schema/tooling features.
[08:42] [08:45] Priya: One weird transcription note: earlier we saw "KV cache" in speaker notes spelled as K-V cache, sometimes 'K V' - minor.
[08:52] Alex: (laughs) yes our docs vary.
[08:55] [09:00] Sam: Wrapping up - recommended pilot: 1-week structured output validation on a subset of production traffic, strict mode ON, human-review for failures, and triage-service integration.
[09:12] Jordan: That sounds good. We'll need the security docs and estimated costs to get budget sign-off.
[09:18] Alex: We'll send SOC2 summary + integration guide and a proposed pilot SOW.
[09:23] Lena: Can we have a demo recording?
[09:25] Alex: Yes, we'll share recording and the repo snippets.
[09:28] [09:30] End recap and next steps repeated.
